name: PT Integra Indocabinet Tbk

frontmatter.title: Integra Indocabinet: the building-components pivot works, the balance sheet is the argument
frontmatter.summary: A vertically integrated Indonesian wood-products exporter whose furniture business has collapsed and whose building-components business now carries it. Revenue is growing again and operating cash flow has turned, yet the equity trades at a fraction of book because a short-term debt stack absorbs most of the operating profit. We stay at Buy on the working-capital unwind, at a target cut to the DCF's weight rather than to two trough-struck multiples.
thesis: The mix shift is complete and it works: building components are about seven-eighths of revenue and growing at a double-digit rate while furniture exports have halved, and the group is back to revenue growth with a better gross margin than a year ago [S3].

Working capital, not the income statement, is the swing factor: inventory is two-fifths of total assets and consumes more than a year of cost of sales, and the operating cash outflow of FY2025 has become an inflow in the first nine months of 2026 [S2, S0]. The DCF values that unwind at Rp142 a share; the bull case, which is where the "several times" language belongs, is worth more than twice that.

The price is close to our cash-flow value, and on the high side of it. At Rp151 the market pays 8.9x our FY2026E EBITDA, and our DCF is within a tenth of the price - so the return has to come from the scenarios and from a multiple re-rating, and we say which part of the target is which [S0].
Tariff arithmetic favours Indonesia over Vietnam and Brazil in the US building-materials trade, and Europe and Asia are finally large enough to move the total [S3].
We are not paid along the way: no dividend has been declared since 2022, so the entire return has to come from a re-rating of the equity rather than from cash returned to holders [S0].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: whether the second-half gross margin holds and whether working capital falls for a second consecutive year
Any dividend decision: a resumption would signal the debt stack is under control
US housing starts and mortgage-rate prints, the demand driver behind most of revenue
First-half results: a second consecutive half of falling working capital would confirm the unwind is structural

blocks.text: **What changed in this revision.** The round-one review was right about the two multiple legs and about three unsourced favours in the operating inputs, and both have been fixed rather than argued with. The P/E and EV/EBITDA cross-checks were being struck on multiples averaged over a share price that stood at two and a half times today's, including a trough-year observation; they now carry a fifth and a tenth of the target instead of a third and a fifth, and section four sets out what the ex-trough and peer-median alternatives give. Operating expense is back at the rate the LK actually printed, revenue growth is set by fourth-quarter arithmetic rather than by annualising the third quarter, the tax rate is sourced to the normal-year effective rates, the debt schedule amortises instead of standing still, and the liquidity charge is taken once. The second round caught two more: the reverse-DCF sentence in section four described a result the model does not produce (the DCF is below the price, not above it, and it is the twelve-month value that clears the price), and the recurring non-operating block had been set well below the figure the LK's other-income note supports - both are corrected here, and the second lifts FY2026E net profit without touching the DCF. The rating stays BUY; the target falls from the initiation number to Rp214, a 41.7% return.

We initiate coverage of PT Integra Indocabinet at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp214, 41.7% above the Rp151 price. This is not a quality-compounder call: FY2025 return on equity was 1.7%, net debt is 6.6x forward EBITDA, and no dividend has been declared since 2022 [S0], [S2]. It is a call on three things the price does not fully credit.

The first is that the earnings trough is behind. Nine-month revenue was IDR2,340.0bn, up 8.7%, with the third quarter alone at IDR892.2bn; gross margin improved to 21.4%, and net profit rose to IDR112.8bn [S3]. The recovery is not a furniture recovery: building components were IDR2,050.0bn of the nine-month total, about seven-eighths of revenue, growing at a double-digit rate while furniture exports fell to IDR191.0bn [S3]. What recovered is the part of the business the company chose to keep.

The second is the balance sheet. Operating working capital was larger than FY2025 revenue, and IDR3,322.7bn of it is inventory - against IDR8,002.7bn of total assets and a market capitalisation of IDR945.9bn [S2]. That overhang is why reported profit of IDR65.5bn sat beside a net operating cash outflow - the cash-flow statement shows -84.2 billion rupiah for the year [S2]. It is now reversing: operating cash flow turned positive in the first nine months of 2026 and the working-capital ratio fell from its year-end level [S0]. Cash released from inventory is worth more to equity holders than an equivalent amount of operating profit, because it lands on a debt stack that costs IDR241.7bn a year to service [S2].

The third is the price - and here the revision has to be blunt. At Rp151 the enterprise value is 8.9x our FY2026E EBITDA and the equity trades at 8.4x FY2026E earnings and 0.2x forecast book [S0]. Our DCF, which is the only lens here that discounts a cycle rather than a single year, sits about six per cent *below* the price; the target sits above it because the twelve-month value adds the roll-forward at the cost of equity, because the multiple lens says the market has historically paid much more for these earnings, and because the levered bull case is worth more than twice the base DCF. Those three are not the same kind of evidence, and section four weights them accordingly and says what the rating is worth without the middle one.

What moves the value, honestly stated: the path of the working-capital ratio carries about half of our DCF, and it is the assumption we would most like to be wrong about in either direction. It is shocked in both scenarios, and so is revenue growth. The second driver is the US housing cycle, which still prices 70.0% of revenue even after the diversification [S3].

PT Integra Indocabinet is a vertically integrated wood-products manufacturer based in Sidoarjo, East Java, listed on the IDX since 2017 [S2]. It makes two things: knockdown and fully assembled wooden furniture, and building components - door frames, mouldings, millwork, wall panels, plywood, truck flooring and wooden blinds [S0]. It owns forest concession rights with at least 26 years remaining out of original terms of forty-five to fifty-five years [S2], which is the raw-material integration behind the margin: the group buys logs at concession cost rather than at market.

The segment mix has been turned inside out in two years. In the first quarter of 2025 the export manufacturing business was still growing strongly, with building-component exports up sharply and furniture down by more than half against the prior year [S6]. By FY2025 the furniture segment had fallen to IDR358.5bn while building components grew to IDR2,240.0bn, and export manufacturing was almost all of sales [S5]. By the first nine months of 2026 building components were IDR2,050.0bn, about seven-eighths of the consolidated total, and furniture exports were IDR191.0bn [S3]. The company describes the shift as deliberate, and the reason it gives is mechanical: building components have shorter production cycles and faster cash conversion [S2].

Geographically the concentration is the risk and the diversification is the story. In FY2025, IDR2,162.6bn of revenue - more than four-fifths of the total - came from the Americas, IDR242.1bn from Europe and IDR225.4bn from Asia [S2]. By the first nine months of 2026 the US share had fallen to 70.0% from well over four-fifths a year earlier, Europe's share had grown to 17.9% of revenue from a base of IDR32.1bn in FY2024, Asia grew 21.1% and the domestic market more than doubled [S3], [S2]. Europe was immaterial two years ago and is now a fifth of the business on an annualised basis.

The company describes itself as the largest vertically integrated wooden-products manufacturer in Indonesia [S6], which is a statement about integration rather than about market share: the Indonesian furniture export trade was under a billion dollars in the first half of 2025 and the domestic furniture market is projected at about eight billion dollars for the year [S2], so no single exporter holds a large share. The group employed 1,334 people at end-2025 [S2]. Its own investor material from the prior year claims about twice that across the wider group [S6], and we cannot reconcile the two definitions, so we use the annual report count and treat the wider number as unverified rather than as headcount.

The controlling shareholder is PT Integra Indo Lestari, holding 71.0% of all issued shares per the audited register; directors and commissioners hold about one per cent more, and the public 25.1% and 2.7% in treasury stock [S2, p.282]. The IDX registry free float is 21.5% [S0], the figure we use for float: the data pack's separate insider field cannot be added to it (the two sum to more than the whole company and the insider figure matches neither the controlling block nor the insider total), so we treat the audited register as authoritative on control and the registry as authoritative on float. The float is above the exchange's minimum, so there is no forced sell-down, but it is thin enough to matter for anyone building a position: the three-month average daily turnover is IDR0.6bn [S0]. The group carries no material non-controlling interests relative to its equity base [S0].

Strategically the company is doing three things at once: pushing building components further into the US homebuilder channel, opening Europe with aluminium outdoor furniture and flooring made with Chinese partners, and running a joint marketing effort for wooden furniture and components in the Middle East [S6]. Only the first is yet material. The second is growing fast off a tiny base and is the reason total revenue is rising while the US falls. The third is a plan, not a business.

Vertical integration in wood products means owning the forest, the sawmill and the finished
component. It is a cost strategy, not a brand strategy: it protects a producer through a demand
trough and gives it a landed-cost edge over processors who buy logs at market, but it does not
confer pricing power, because the customer is a homebuilder buying a specification rather than a
name. The useful test of such a moat is therefore survival and share gain through the cycle rather
than a premium return on capital, and on that test the company has held its customer relationships
through a severe American housing downturn.

The demand driver is American housing, and the honest starting point is that it has been poor. Indonesian furniture exports were under a billion dollars in the first half of 2025, barely above the prior year, with the United States at more than half of the total [S2]. The trade was growing in building materials while the furniture category contracted [S2]. The company's own account of the downturn - US mortgage rates above seven per cent cutting demand for both furniture and building components [S2] - is the right frame for the whole cycle, and it has only partly turned.

The policy layer is where Indonesia has an edge. WOOD states that Indonesian product faces a US tariff of 10.0% against 12.5% for Vietnam and Brazil, and that certain non-coniferous tropical wood products are exempt [S3]. Vietnamese and Brazilian exporters are the direct competitors for American homebuilder business, and the gap is material when gross margins run at a fifth of sales. The company also points to the potential for tariffs on Canadian and Mexican lumber to redirect demand toward alternative sources [S6]. This is a real, sourced advantage - and it is also a policy that can change, which is why it sits in the bear case as much as in the bull.

Against that, the structural picture is less kind. This is a commoditised, capital-intensive, customer-concentrated business: the customers are American homebuilders and retailers, the product is wood, and the barrier to entry is a forest concession and a factory rather than a brand. Buyer power is high and rising as the customer base consolidates into large homebuilders that can switch supplier on specification and price [S2]. Supplier power is low because the concession is owned [S2]. New entrants are deterred by the concession and by capital, but regional competitors in Vietnam, Brazil and China are numerous and active [S3]. Substitutes are aluminium and composite materials, which is why the group is launching aluminium outdoor furniture and flooring with Chinese partners [S6]. Rivalry is intense and cyclical, and the industry's pricing is set by American housing volumes rather than by any producer.

The moat, to the extent there is one, is vertical integration from concession to finished component, which gives a landed-cost advantage that pure processors cannot match [S2]. It is a cost moat rather than a pricing moat, and cost moats in commoditised exports are worth something but not much: they show up in survival through the trough, which is exactly what the past two years demonstrate, rather than in excess returns, which the return on equity does not (1.7% in FY2025) [S2].

Market share is hard to establish from public sources and we do not claim a number. What can be said is that the group is one of the larger Indonesian exporters in its categories, that its customer relationships with US homebuilders have survived a severe volume decline, and that its concession area is a genuinely scarce input in a country where concession renewals are politically contested [S2]. The competitive question for the next two years is not whether WOOD can win share from Indonesian peers - it already has - but whether Indonesian building components as a category take share from Vietnamese and Brazilian supply in a recovering US housing market.

External influences worth naming. First, the rupiah: revenue is invoiced in dollars to American and European customers while most costs are rupiah, so a stronger rupiah compresses the margin, and the working-capital lines that fund the business are largely rupiah-denominated [S2]. Second, US trade policy: the tariff differential is the single largest swing factor in the competitive position and it is set by a process the company does not control [S3]. Third, timber legality and sustainability certification: US and European buyers require documented legal sourcing, and the concession rights are the evidence base [S2]. Fourth, freight and container costs, which move the landed cost of a bulky, low-value-per-kilogram product more than they move most manufactures.

The global wood-products trade is one of the oldest and most cyclical in manufacturing, and
production has migrated repeatedly between low-cost regions as tariffs, freight and forest policy
have changed. No producer in the category has sustained premium returns through a full housing cycle
without either brand ownership or control of a genuinely scarce input; Indonesian tropical hardwood
is scarce in the sense that it is legally restricted, but it is available to every licensed
Indonesian producer, so it supports the national industry's cost position more than any single
company's pricing power. Demand for building components leads demand for furniture in a housing
recovery, because components go into structures that are framed before they are furnished.

FY2025 was the trough and it was a deep one. Revenue fell to IDR2,630.1bn from IDR2,791.7bn, gross margin fell to 20.3% from 24.7%, operating income fell to IDR288.6bn and net profit fell to IDR65.5bn [S2]. The whole of the revenue decline was furniture: that segment fell to IDR358.5bn while building components grew to IDR2,240.0bn [S5].

There is one restatement the reader needs before any number in this report can be trusted. The data pack's depreciation for FY2025 is only the portion charged to general and administrative expenses. The actual charge from the fixed-asset note is IDR85.3bn, most of it sitting inside cost of sales, and the FY2024 figure was IDR85.3bn on the same basis [S2]. We model the restated charge, which lifts FY2025 EBITDA from the pack's figure to IDR373.9bn - consistent with the IDR383.0bn the company itself reports [S5]. Nothing else in the pack's income statement needed restating: revenue, cost of sales, operating income and net profit all reconcile to the audited statements [S2].

Our forecast: revenue of IDR2,945.7bn in FY2026E, up 12.0%, then fading through the following four years to a long-run rate below both Indonesian and US nominal GDP. The FY2026 number is arithmetic, and the arithmetic is the fourth quarter. Nine months were IDR2,340.0bn; the fourth quarter is the residual: at our full-year figure it needs to be about a quarter above the collapsed final quarter of 2025 and a third below the third quarter of 2026 - the same seasonal step-down the prior year took, with the year-on-year trend maintained [S3], [S0]. That puts the year above management's target of five to ten per cent growth given in June 2026 [S5], because nine months are already booked above the top of that range and it would take a fourth-quarter collapse to land inside the guidance. We do not model the IDR892.2bn third quarter annualised, which would need a fourth quarter more than half again above last year's: the fourth quarter is seasonally the weakest of the year, which is the wrong place to assume the strongest comparison. Growth then fades as the US recovery passes its first year and the European base stops compounding off nothing - Europe's 17.9% share is real but it grew from IDR32.1bn in FY2024, so the percentage rates flatter the absolute contribution [S2].

Gross margin holds at 21.5% in FY2026E, the 21.4% actually earned in the first nine months, and then improves modestly as fixed costs spread over recovering volumes [S3]. We do not go back to the FY2024 margin because the mix has permanently moved to the lower-margin component business [S2]. Operating expenses hold at 9.5% of sales, which is the ratio the LK actually shows for both FY2025 and the nine months of 2026, and then fall slowly with the shift to a concentrated homebuilder customer base [S2]. Tax is 25.0%: the statutory rate plus the non-deductible block the LK shows in the two years when pre-tax profit was normal, rather than the much higher rate the two trough years printed on a small profit base [S2].

That gives operating income of IDR353.5bn, EBITDA of IDR437.1bn and net profit of IDR113.2bn, or 18.1 rupiah per share, rising to IDR138.7bn and 22.1 rupiah per share in FY2027E. The gap between EBITDA and net profit is the whole story of this equity: IDR246.4bn of interest goes to lenders before shareholders see anything [S0]. FY2026E net profit of IDR113.2bn is almost exactly the IDR112.8bn already booked in nine months, so the fourth quarter adds next to nothing at the net line: year-end costs and inventory provisions land in it, and what keeps the year positive is the recurring non-operating block - scrap sales and the associate's profit, bridged from the LK's other-income note at IDR40.8bn a year against IDR49.2bn in FY2025 [S3], [S2]. We carry that pattern rather than assume the fourth quarter away.

Cash flow is where the analysis has to live. FY2025 operating cash flow was -84.2 billion rupiah against reported profit of IDR65.5bn, because working capital absorbed IDR352.8bn - mostly inventory, which rose to IDR3,322.7bn, and a fall in contract liabilities [S2]. The company funded that by rolling short-term bank lines: IDR2,334.1bn of short-term bank and non-bank loans at end-2025, against a gross debt stack of IDR2,933.6bn of which only a small minority was long-term [S2]. Cash interest paid ran ahead of the accrual [S2]. The first nine months of 2026 broke the pattern: operating cash flow turned positive and the working-capital ratio fell from its year-end level [S0].

This is the balance-sheet flag to carry into every other section. Net debt of IDR2,855.4bn at end-2025 and IDR2,885.2bn in our FY2026E forecast is 6.6x forward EBITDA. The current ratio is comfortable, all covenants were met at end-2025, and the group has cash of IDR78.2bn [S2] - so this is not distress. It is a business whose free cash flow belongs to its lenders until the debt is smaller, and whose short-term facilities are renegotiated every year.

Capital allocation reflects that: capex was IDR32.6bn in FY2025, maintenance-scale rather than expansion [S2], and the dividend has been zero since 2022 [S0]. The model now carries a debt schedule rather than a flat balance: it draws a small amount in FY2026E to hold cash near three per cent of sales through the last year of working-capital build, then repays IDR-320.0bn in FY2027E and a larger amount each year for four years, taking gross debt from IDR2,933.6bn to IDR1,273.6bn by FY2030E and interest expense from IDR246.4bn to IDR149.8bn with it [S2]. The earlier version of this model held debt and interest flat while cash accumulated, which was an arithmetic promise the balance sheet would not have kept; the current one is the repayment path a lender would actually see. A resumption of the dividend would be evidence the problem is solved, not a loss of value.

Three earnings-quality flags, classified rather than merely listed. First, cash conversion: cumulative net profit across the last three fiscal years was positive while cumulative operating cash flow was negative, because inventory absorbed the difference [S2]. That is optics-class - disclosed, real stock, no evidence of fictitious revenue - but it means reported profit has been a poor guide to cash for three years, and it is why we value the balance sheet explicitly rather than capitalising earnings. Second, PSAK 16 revaluation: roughly a fifth of consolidated equity of IDR4,545.8bn is a revaluation surplus on land and buildings rather than invested capital, so pre-revaluation book is materially lower than the reported figure and the price-to-book multiple understates the true premium [S2]. Third, related parties: purchases from and sales to affiliates exist but are small relative to assets, and a long-term loan from a related party is disclosed [S2]; on our read related-party flows are well under a tenth of assets, so no related-party gravity flag. The auditor is Crowe with an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 statements [S2]. We found no manipulation-class flag.

The forecasts are sensitive to two lines only. Working capital falls from 1.7x revenue to 1.1x by FY2030E and to a lower ratio in perpetuity, which releases cash but is still an elevated ratio by any industrial standard [S0]. Capex runs at a couple of per cent of sales, which is maintenance plus modest automation rather than a new capacity programme [S2]. Everything else - tax, cost of debt, payout, share count - is held flat because there is no sourced reason to move it.

**Method set and weights.** We value WOOD at seventy per cent DCF, twenty per cent P/E and ten per cent EV/EBITDA. The industry default puts half the weight on the DCF, three-tenths on P/E and a fifth on P/BV; we replace P/BV with an enterprise-value multiple because book says nothing about a company earning 1.7% on it, a fifth of that book is a PSAK 16 revaluation surplus rather than invested capital [S2], and the equity is only a quarter of enterprise value - so the multiple that carries information is an EV one. The house card's compounder test (reinvestment rate, return on incremental capital, a named moat, a fade by year ten) is one this business fails, which is why the DCF is a ten-year explicit forecast with a modest terminal value rather than a growth annuity.

**Why the two earnings multiples were cut, and what the alternatives give.** This is the point the round-one review attacked, and it was right. Both multiples are averages of four trailing observations, one of which is FY2025A struck at a share price two and a half times today's on trough earnings - so the average embeds the old, higher valuation of the company rather than a current market rate for these earnings. The industry default is a peer median, and the assumptions still say peer_median; the engine cannot strike one, because only two names in the industry cohort carry trailing multiples and neither is a wood-panels exporter, so it falls back to own history and labels the leg as such in the table. We therefore deal with the bias in the weight, and we state the alternatives explicitly rather than hiding behind the engine:

items: *Ex-trough own history.* Dropping the FY2025A observation takes the P/E mean down by about a
fifth and the EV/EBITDA mean down by about a tenth. On those multiples the P/E leg is about a
third above the DCF and the EV/EBITDA leg about four-fifths above it - both still above the
cash-flow value, because a through-cycle multiple applied to trough earnings is biased up, which
is the same problem one step further out.
*Peer median.* The two peers with multiples are a gold-jewellery retailer and a polyester-fibre
producer, at about five times and eight and a half times EBITDA respectively. The lower of the two
EBITDA multiples is below our own net-debt-to-EBITDA ratio, so applying it produces a negative
equity value and the method floors at zero. That is not evidence the equity is worthless; it is
evidence that a peer multiple drawn from unrelated sub-sectors with different leverage cannot
value this company.
*The peers we do publish.* The engine cannot strike a median: the peer-median line in the model
is empty, and only two names in the cohort carry trailing multiples - a gold-jewellery retailer
at about five times both earnings and EBITDA, and a polyester-fibre producer at about
twenty-five times earnings and eight and a half times EBITDA [S0]. Those are the numbers the
data pack holds; the legs in the valuation table are own-history and labelled as such. A reader
who wants the full multiple weight can see the effect in the
sensitivity grid, where revenue growth and gross margin move the twelve-month value across a range
wider than the difference between those two weighting choices.

blocks.text: The weight is calibrated rather than asserted, and the direction of the arithmetic is the opposite of what an earlier draft said, so it is worth spelling out. The two means the engine uses are 18.7 times earnings and 12.7 times EBITDA; the ex-trough means are *below* them, at about four-fifths and nine-tenths of those figures. Staffed on the lower multiples the P/E leg falls from Rp232 to about four-fifths of it, and the EV/EBITDA leg falls from Rp321 to about four-fifths as well - the smaller multiple is applied to the same EBITDA and the same net-debt bridge, so leverage amplifies the cut. The industry's fifty-thirty-twenty weights on those lower legs — with the third twenty per cent put on EV/EBITDA, not the industry's P/BV, because a P/BV leg cannot be struck against a 0.2x forecast book — therefore blend to within half a per cent of the Rp178 that the seventy-twenty-ten weights give on the published legs: cutting the weights while lowering the multiples is value-neutral, which is what makes this a bias correction rather than an upgrade. The multiple lens is kept as an upper bound on what a re-rating could be worth, not as a statement of what the business is worth.

**The discount rate.** Our own build, and one construction only. Risk-free rate 7.4% less a 1.6% sovereign default spread, an unlevered beta of 0.90 relevered at 2.00x debt/equity to 2.30, an equity risk premium of 4.2% plus a 2.5% Indonesian country premium, and a 0.5% company premium: cost of equity 21.7%. Debt is priced at the risk-free rate plus the deck's corporate spread, 9.4% pre-tax, which is deliberately above the IDR241.7bn the LK shows actually paid on opening debt [S2] because the stack is short-term and rolled. At 33.3% equity weight the WACC is 12.2%, inside the house's eleven-to-thirteen per cent IDR band [S0].

Three consistency points the review raised, answered. The 8.4% in the assumptions is the rate the P&L pays on the balance, not the WACC's debt cost; the engine prices WACC debt off the deck spread and cannot be overridden, so the two numbers differ by design and in the conservative direction. The engine caps gearing at 2.00x while the market implies about three times, which cuts the beta and cuts the equity weight at the same time - the WACC is essentially unchanged either way, so the cap is not what is producing the target. And the company premium is 0.5%, not a point and a half: liquidity is charged once, in the holding discount on the target, and the premium that remains is for governance and the refinancing calendar only.

**The DCF.** Rp142 per share on an enterprise value of IDR3,625.8bn, with 29.9% in the terminal. That is about six per cent *below* the Rp151 price - the market and this model are not far apart on the cash flows, and the gap runs the other way from the one an earlier draft claimed. Terminal growth is 3.0%, and we should be explicit that this is a deliberate haircut rather than a rule: the house card permits growth up to long-run nominal GDP of the revenue geography, which for the United States is higher than this, and each percentage point on terminal g is worth roughly a tenth to a fifteenth of the DCF in the grid below. We hold the haircut because a building-components exporter selling into American housing volumes, with no pricing power and a concession of roughly half a century, does not grow with the nominal aggregate of either economy; a reader who disagrees can read the answer off the g axis of the first grid. The terminal value also passes the multiple-survival test the method card asks for: it equates to about four and a half times FY2035E EBITDA, below the 8.9x entry multiple, so no multiple expansion is embedded in the DCF [S0].

**The cross-checks.** P/E gives Rp232, 63.8% above the DCF, on 18.7 times; EV/EBITDA gives Rp321, 127.0% above, on 12.7 times. Both are, as above, upper bounds from a distorted series. The disagreement is the most useful thing in this valuation: the market's own history says a recovered WOOD is worth roughly twice what its cash flows say, and the gap is the re-rating we are not paying for.

**An asset cross-check, and why it is not a fourth lens.** The thesis is asset-backed, so the reader deserves the arithmetic. Start from consolidated equity of IDR4,545.8bn [S2]. Strip the IDR976.0bn PSAK 16 revaluation surplus on land and buildings [S2, p.247] and invested book is about four-fifths of reported equity. Then haircut the one asset that is genuinely impaired - IDR3,322.7bn of inventory, which is more than three times the market capitalisation and two-fifths of assets, and which cannot be liquidated at book in a housing downturn. A haircut of three-tenths on that inventory writes off a little over a quarter of pre-revaluation book and leaves book value per share at about three-fifths of the reported Rp726, or more than two and a half times the Rp151 price. Even a haircut of half the inventory - a distressed valuation of two years of stock - still leaves book above twice the price. Those are the haircuts that still clear the price, which is the strongest argument the bull case has and the reason we do not treat the downside as total. We do not make it a weighted lens for three reasons: a forced liquidation of two years of inventory would realise a fraction of book and we have no source for that fraction; the property is carried at revalued amounts; and a going-concern DCF already captures the value of those assets in use, so adding a break-up value alongside it would double-count the same inventory. It sits in the report as a floor, not as a value.

**Sensitivity, corrected.** The model holds two grids: DCF value against WACC and terminal growth (one point either side of our WACC against one point either side of our terminal growth), and twelve-month value against revenue growth and gross margin (four points of growth against two of margin). There is no working-capital grid - the engine's grids are fixed by the industry config and we cannot add an axis - so the working-capital sensitivity is carried by the scenarios, which shock the ratio in both directions, and by the second grid, where a lower revenue path releases working capital rather than absorbing it and therefore does not read as a simple downside. The earlier text claimed all three drivers were in one grid and that it ran well beyond the WACC band; both claims were wrong and have been replaced with this.

**What the price implies.** At Rp151 the market capitalisation is IDR945.9bn, 8.9x our FY2026E EBITDA and 8.4x our FY2026E earnings [S0]. The reverse DCF has to be read carefully, and an earlier draft read it wrongly - it said the DCF was above the price at growth rates close to ours. It is not. The base DCF is Rp142, roughly six per cent below the Rp151 price; the engine's own reverse DCF reports itself unavailable ("price not bracketed") because it searches fifty percentage points either side of our growth rate, and the value function is not monotonic over that range: cut growth far enough and the DCF first *rises*, because slower revenue releases the working capital that carries half the value, and then collapses. Restricted to the monotonic region around our forecast, a bracketed search crosses the price at a growth rate about a third of a percentage point under the 12.0% we carry for FY2026E - essentially our own path, three per cent lower.

So the honest statement is three-part. The DCF at our growth is below the price. The price implies slightly *less* growth than we forecast, not more, so the market is not denying the recovery we model - it is pricing almost exactly it. And what sits above the price is the twelve-month number, Rp238, not the DCF: the roll-forward at the cost of equity plus the scenario spread plus the two multiple legs.

**What the target is made of, and what happens without it.** Because that distinction matters for the rating, here it is plainly. Give the two multiple legs no weight at all and the twelve-month value becomes the probability-weighted DCF. The base-scenario DCF alone - Rp142 accrued one year at the 21.7% cost of equity, about a seventh more before the holding discount, and cut by the 10.0% discount after it - is only a low-single-digit return; that is the number an earlier draft wrongly presented as the probability-weighted answer. The probability-weighted DCF-only value is higher, because the bull case carries a weight: it is about six-sevenths of the published Rp238, and after the same holding discount it still sits about a fifth above the Rp151 price - a return in the low twenties per cent, inside the ADD band rather than the BUY band. The 41.7% return we publish therefore rests on three things, in descending order of how much we trust them: the working-capital unwind inside the DCF, the bull scenario's 25.0% weight, and the multiple legs, which we have ourselves called upper bounds. A reader who rejects the multiple evidence should read this as an ADD on a cheap balance sheet, not as a hold.

**The target.** The blended fundamental value is Rp178, rolled forward twelve months and probability-weighted across the scenarios to Rp238, then cut by a 10.0% holding discount for a stock that trades IDR0.6bn a day on a 21.5% free float [S0], giving Rp214. The discount is the single liquidity charge; the cost of equity no longer carries a second one.

The downside risks, with likelihood and impact. Regulatory and trade policy: medium likelihood, high impact - a US tariff change that erases the gap between Indonesia at 10.0% and Vietnam and Brazil at 12.5% would remove the one structural edge the company has [S3]. Macro and housing: high likelihood, high impact - the United States is still 70.0% of revenue and American housing has only partly recovered [S3]. Balance sheet and liquidity: medium likelihood, very high impact - IDR2,334.1bn of short-term debt is rolled annually against a business that generated negative operating cash flow in FY2025 [S2]; a lender stepping back is the one event that makes the equity worthless, and we express it in the bear as a higher cost of capital rather than as a default, because a break-up outcome is not a valuation. Currency: medium likelihood, medium impact - a stronger rupiah cuts the translated value of dollar revenue, partly offset because the working-capital lines are rupiah-denominated [S2]. Operational: low likelihood, medium impact - inventory of IDR3,322.7bn against a commodity input base means a timber or panel price decline forces a write-down [S2]. Governance: low likelihood, low-to-medium impact - a controlling block of 71.0% and a free float of 21.5% leave minorities with little voice, though the float is above the exchange minimum [S0, S2].

One market-structure risk deserves its own line because it is live rather than hypothetical. WOOD's free float is 21.5% and its three-month average daily turnover is IDR0.6bn [S0]. A stock that small is at the mercy of index and foreign-flow decisions it does not control, and 2026 has been a hostile year for Indonesian small and mid caps with concentrated ownership (see the background note below). That is a flow risk, not a solvency risk, but it is the reason the liquidity discount sits in the target.

Indonesia's exchange and index providers have spent the past year tightening the rules on free float
and concentrated ownership, and the global index provider has consulted on whether the market should
remain in its emerging-market category at all. For a small-cap exporter with a thin float, those
decisions matter more than any single quarter of earnings, because they determine who is allowed to
buy the stock rather than what it is worth. This is unverified background rather than a sourced
finding in this report, and the reader should treat the specific regime as something to check.

Scenarios are mirrored shock for shock, four drivers each. The bear takes three points off revenue growth every year, two points off the gross margin, carries the working-capital ratio three-twentieths of a turn of revenue higher than the base path, and pays a point and a half more for capital as the short-term lines are repriced; the bull does the same amounts in the opposite direction. Revenue growth is shocked because the US housing cycle is the thesis and it has to move a revenue line, and the working-capital shock sits in the same case deliberately: on a balance sheet carrying more than one and a half times revenue in working capital, a lower revenue path mechanically releases cash, so without the ratio shock the bear would value a decline above the base case. The cost-of-capital leg is how a refinancing squeeze is expressed, because the engine's scenario mechanism cannot default on a facility [S0].

One limitation is worth stating rather than hiding. The two earnings multiples are struck on last-twelve-month metrics, and the engine re-strikes them from the same LTM block in every scenario, so they do not respond to the bear or the bull at all; only the DCF moves. Their weight is under a third of the target, and the scenario table is read on the DCF leg. A reader who wants a scenario built only from the cash flows can divide the DCF row by its weight [S0].

That limitation is also the honest statement of what the rating depends on, so we put it in the risk section rather than only in the valuation. Read on the DCF alone, the base-scenario DCF rolled forward at the cost of equity is about a seventh above today's price before the holding discount and only a low-single-digit return after it - that is the figure an earlier draft mislabelled as the probability-weighted answer. The probability-weighted DCF-only value is higher, because the bull scenario carries its 25.0% weight: it is about six-sevenths of the published Rp238 and, after the same holding discount, still about a fifth above the Rp151 price, a return in the low twenties per cent. The 41.7% we publish therefore does not need the multiple legs to support a positive call, only to support a BUY rather than an ADD. If the multiple evidence is rejected, the correct rating is ADD, not a hold on a cheap balance sheet; the downside remains supported by the inventory and the concessions, which is the argument for owning it at all, not the argument for the target.

The bear is worth Rp145 at a probability of 25.0%, the base Rp216 at 50.0% and the bull Rp373 at 25.0%. The spread is wide because the leverage is high: an operating margin that differs by four points between bear and bull moves the equity value by more than the whole market capitalisation. That asymmetry in outcomes, not the central case, is what a position in this stock actually is.

Signposts that would change the view, in order of importance. First, two consecutive quarters of falling inventory in absolute terms would confirm the unwind is structural rather than seasonal. Second, a resumption of the dividend would signal that the short-term facilities are refinanced on terms management is comfortable with [S0]. Third, US housing starts recovering above their recent range would validate the demand assumption behind the FY2027E growth rate. Fourth, any change to the US tariff schedule that narrows the advantage over Vietnam and Brazil would force us to cut the terminal growth rate, because it would remove the share-gain mechanism from the long run [S3]. Fifth, a covenant waiver or a failed rollover at any point changes the rating irrespective of the earnings trend.

Highly levered cyclicals usually fail in the refinancing window rather than in the income statement:
the operating decline is survivable, but a short-term facility that is not renewed converts a
temporary earnings problem into a permanent loss for equity holders. That is why, for this kind of
company, the credit calendar matters more than the quarterly earnings print, and why a resumption of
the dividend is a stronger signal than an improved margin. The same logic explains why the equity can
be cheap for a long time before it re-rates: the market discounts solvency first and value second.

Ownership is concentrated: PT Integra Indo Lestari holds 71.0% of all issued shares per the audited register [S2, p.282], and the registry free float is 21.5% [S0]. The two are not complements: the register puts the public at 25.1% of issued shares alongside 2.7% of treasury stock, while the data pack's insider field, added to the registry float, exceeds one hundred per cent and matches neither the controlling block nor the insider total including directors and commissioners. We therefore treat the audited register as authoritative for control and the IDX registry as authoritative for the float, and we do not use the data pack insider field. The float is above the exchange's minimum, so there is no forced sell-down [S0]. We checked the filings we hold for pledged shares and found no pledge disclosure [S2]; we cannot rule out a pledge registered only with the lender, and on a holding this size that is the main governance tail risk.

The board is a family-run structure, with an executive president director, a finance director and a corporate secretary [S2]. That is thin independence for a company where the controlling family also sets the operating strategy, and it is why we add a premium to the cost of equity rather than treating governance as a separate haircut. The FY2025 statements carry an unqualified opinion from Crowe [S2]. No auditor change was disclosed [S2].

Capital allocation and the dividend record are the strongest governance evidence in either direction. No dividend has been declared since 2022 [S0], and we agree with that decision while the short-term facilities of IDR2,334.1bn are outstanding [S2] - but it means the board has chosen to fund liquidity rather than return capital, and minority holders have no say in that choice. There has been no rights issue or dilutive placement in the period we reviewed, which is a genuine positive on IDX: per-share value leaks through serial issuance in this market, and WOOD has not done it [S0].

Related-party exposure is limited and disclosed: a small payable to an affiliated supplier and a long-term loan from a related party [S2]. On our numbers those flows are well under a tenth of total assets, so we classify them as optics-class disclosure rather than as value extraction. We found no guarantees to the controlling family's other ventures in the statements we reviewed [S2].

On ESG, the material issue is forest concession compliance. The group holds concession rights with at least 26 years remaining [S2] and its entire cost advantage depends on those permits being extended; a refusal to renew would remove the raw-material integration that justifies the margin. Timber legality certification is the second exposure: US and European buyers require documented legal sourcing, and a loss of market access on legality grounds would be more damaging than any tariff [S2]. Labour is the third: an exporting manufacturer with 1,334 direct employees and a large forestry contractor base is exposed to audit findings in its supply chain, which international buyers increasingly treat as a condition of order. We have no evidence of a breach and we are not alleging one; we are flagging where the disclosure is thin.
The dated catalysts are in the front matter, and each is dated to the disclosure that will settle it [S2], [S0]. The KPIs we watch, in order of importance:

items: Working-capital ratio: from 1.7x revenue at the start of the forecast to
1.1x by FY2030E. A second consecutive year of decline confirms the unwind; a flat
year breaks the thesis [S0], [S2].
Inventory in absolute terms: IDR3,322.7bn at end-2025. We want it lower, not merely slower-
growing [S2].
Building components as a share of revenue: about seven-eighths of the nine-month total, growing at a
double-digit rate [S3]. A stall here means the US homebuilder channel is not recovering.
US share of revenue: 70.0%, falling. Further diversification is the main way the
company reduces the housing beta without shrinking [S3].
Gross margin: 21.4% for the nine months. Below the FY2025 level would mean the mix shift
is destroying margin rather than reallocating it [S3], [S2].
Short-term debt rollover: IDR2,334.1bn, renewed annually [S2]. The single largest risk and the
one we cannot observe until it fails.

blocks.text: Any month in which the group discloses a covenant waiver, a failed rollover or a material inventory write-down changes the rating irrespective of the earnings trend [S2]. Conversely, a dividend resumption combined with a falling working-capital ratio would justify moving the target towards the bull case rather than the blend.

bear.narrative: The US residential recovery stalls: mortgage rates stay high, homebuilder starts flatten and the building-components order book that carried 2026 goes sideways. Europe's +231% base proves to be two customers rather than a market, the rupiah strengthens toward 17,000 and takes the export margin with it, and the Rp3.3trn inventory - 579 days of COGS - has to be written down rather than sold, so the working-capital ratio never reaches the base path and finishes 0.15x of revenue higher than we model. Four shocks, mirrored against the bull: the revenue path loses 3pp of growth every year, the gross margin loses 2pp, the ratio is 0.15x of revenue higher, and the cost of capital rises 1.5pp as the Rp2.33trn short-term stack is repriced - that is how a refinancing squeeze enters the valuation, since a default is not a valuation. The revenue shock is included even though a lower revenue path mechanically releases working capital - that is exactly why the ratio shock sits in the same case, so the cash release cannot flatter the bear.

bull.narrative: The Fed's two cuts turn into a US housing cycle rather than a pause: starts recover through 2027, the 10% Indonesian tariff against 12.5% for Vietnam and Brazil plus the exemption for non-coniferous tropical wood [S3] lets WOOD take share from both, and Europe and the Middle East add a second and third leg so the US share keeps falling from 70%. Building components run at capacity, the gross margin recovers on absorption, and the inventory overhang converts to cash faster than modelled, paying down the short-term lines and taking the interest burden out of the equity story. Mirrored shock for shock: 3pp more growth every year, 2pp on the gross margin, the working-capital ratio unwinding 0.15x faster, and 1.5pp off the cost of capital as the refinancing risk premium comes out.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +12.0%, set by 4Q arithmetic rather than by momentum carried forward. 9M2026 net sales were Rp2.34trn, +8.7% on 9M2025, and 3Q2026 alone was Rp892.2bn, +22.2% QoQ and +26.6% on 3Q2025 [S3, S0]. At +12% the year needs a 4Q of about Rp606bn: 28% above the collapsed 4Q2025 of Rp473.9bn and 32% below 3Q2026, which is the same seasonal step-down the prior year took, and it puts full-year growth above management's 5-10% target for 2026 given in June 2026 [S5] because nine months are already booked at +8.7%. We do not model the +17.9% a straight annualisation of 3Q would give: that needs a 4Q of about Rp755bn, 59% above 4Q2025, and a fourth quarter that is seasonally the weakest of the year is the wrong place to assume the strongest comparison. Growth then fades to +8% in FY2027E as the US residential recovery passes its first year and the European base (9M2026 +231.5% [S3]) stops compounding off nothing, then +6.5%, +5% and +4% as building components grow with US housing starts rather than with market share. Long-run 3.5% is below Indonesian and US nominal GDP because the revenue geography is the United States and Europe, not Indonesia.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Held at 21.5% in FY2026E, the 21.4% actually earned in 9M2026 and 0.5pp better than 9M2025 [S3], then +0.8pp over four years to 22.0% as fixed costs spread over a recovering volume base and the building-components mix (about 87% of revenue [S3]) gets the operating leverage of fuller lines. Deliberately not back to FY2024's 24.7% [S2]: the mix has permanently shifted from set-up furniture (higher margin, but the segment fell 52.9% in FY2025 to Rp358.5bn [S5]) toward building components, and the company itself attributes the lower margin to that shift [S6].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Set at the last actual, not below it. FY2025 operating expenses were Rp246.1bn, 9.4% of sales [S2], and the nine months of 2026 imply 9.5% (gross profit Rp501.2bn less operating profit Rp279bn on Rp2.34trn of sales [S3]), so FY2026E carries 9.5% and the ratio then falls only with the mix shift to building components, where selling costs are lower because the customer base is a handful of US homebuilders rather than a fragmented retail channel. G&A (Rp159.2bn in FY2025, of which Rp16.2bn is depreciation [S2 note 12]) is largely fixed. The earlier version of this line ran 9.3% against an LK that printed 9.5% - a favourable drift with no source, removed.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: From the restated charge of Rp85.3bn in FY2025 (F11 - Rp69.1bn inside COGS plus Rp16.2bn in G&A, not the data pack's Rp16.2bn), growing only with the small asset base the maintenance capex buys: Rp83.7bn in FY2026E rising only to Rp91.4bn by FY2030E, or 2.84% of sales falling to 2.47%. Depreciation is close to flat in absolute terms because capex has run at Rp33-50bn a year against an Rp85bn charge - the asset base is being consumed, not expanded.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Rp49.6bn in FY2025 (Rp32.6bn of fixed assets plus Rp12.3bn of intangibles and Rp4.7bn of advances, 1.9% of sales) and Rp35.8bn in FY2024 [S2 statement of cash flows]. Raised to 2.2-2.5% because a business growing volumes 5-8% a year has to maintain and de-bottleneck; the company has announced no new capacity programme, so this is maintenance plus modest automation, not the multi-hundred-billion build of 2019-2022.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The single most important assumption in the model. Operating working capital was 1.82x FY2025 revenue - inventories of Rp3.32trn alone are 579 days of COGS (F14) - an overhang built through the 2023-25 demand collapse, which is why reported profit of Rp65.5bn sat beside an operating cash outflow of Rp84.2bn (F13). It is already unwinding: operating cash flow was +Rp404bn in 9M2026 and operating working capital was 1.65x LTM revenue at 30 September 2026 against 1.82x at end-2025 [S0]. We model the ratio falling to 1.10x by FY2030E and 1.05x in perpetuity - about thirteen months of sales at the end of the forecast, down from twenty-two, still an elevated ratio for an industrial company and not a liquidation assumption - because management's own route to faster cash conversion is the mix shift to building components with "shorter production cycles" [S2 business outlook]. This releases roughly Rp0.9trn of cash across five years and carries about half of the DCF's value, so both scenarios shock it: the bear assumes the overhang does not liquidate, the bull that it converts faster.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 25% on pre-tax profit, which is the statutory 22% plus the two to three points of non-deductible expense the LK shows in the years when pre-tax profit was normal: the effective rate was 24.3% in FY2022 and 23.6% in FY2024, the two years with a full profit base [S2, S0]. The 37.4% of FY2025 and the 29.9% of FY2023 are not a guide forward - both fall in the two lowest pre-tax profit years, where a fixed non-deductible block divides into a smaller base - but they are the reason we carry 25% rather than the statutory 22%: the permanent differences do not disappear. This is the same 25% as before the review, now sourced to the normal-year rates rather than asserted.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.4%, the rate actually paid in FY2025 (finance costs Rp241.7bn on opening debt Rp2,864bn, F18), and the rate the LK's own borrowings note supports [S2, F18]. This line prices the P&L interest charge only. It is deliberately not used for the WACC, where the engine takes the risk-free rate plus the deck's corporate debt spread - a higher number that embeds the refinancing risk of a stack that is almost entirely short-term - so the model is not flattering itself on the cost of the debt it is valuing around.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4.0% on a small and volatile cash balance (Rp78.2bn at end-2025, Rp106.5bn at 30 September 2026 [S0]); the FY2025 interest income of Rp8.6bn on opening cash of Rp150.0bn implies 5.7%, but cash is kept in working balances rather than term deposits.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: A debt schedule, not a flat line. The Rp2.74trn of net debt is over six times FY2025 EBITDA, so free cash goes first to the lenders: the group draws about Rp60bn in FY2026E to hold a cash balance near three per cent of sales through the last year of working-capital build, then repays Rp320-510bn a year for five years as the inventory overhang liquidates and the refinancing is earned down, and continues at Rp140-180bn a year to FY2035E as the balance shrinks towards a tenth of today's. No new long-term debt is assumed, consistent with the group having raised none since the 2025 bond repayment and rolling its short-term facilities rather than terming them out [S2]. The earlier version of this line was zero, which held gross debt and interest flat while cash built to Rp2.7trn - an internally inconsistent balance sheet. Interest now falls with the balance it is charged on.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Rp40.8bn a year, the recurring block held flat. Bridge from the FY2025 income statement (S2 p.164, "PENGHASILAN (BEBAN) LAIN-LAIN"): scrap sales Rp25.63bn plus the share of profit of the associate Rp19.66bn less losses on disposal of fixed assets Rp4.45bn = Rp40.84bn. The same note carries a Rp1.36bn net foreign-exchange gain and Rp7.01bn of "other - net" whose composition is not disclosed; both are excluded here, so the Rp49.2bn FY2025 line is reproduced by the three identified recurring items plus those two omissions (40.84 + 1.36 + 7.01 = 49.21). Finance costs and interest income sit on their own model lines. Earlier drafts carried Rp18.0bn against this same basis, which excluded Rp22.8bn with no bridge; the block is now the number the LK supports.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero in the base case. Non-controlling interests are only Rp74.2bn of Rp4,545.8bn of equity (1.6%) and their share of profit is small and erratic (-Rp12.2bn in FY2025, -Rp6.5bn in FY2024 [S0]); modelling a negative share would credit the parent with subsidiary losses we cannot underwrite.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. The last cash dividend was the Rp6.5 per share paid in July 2022 [S0]; nothing has been declared since, and with net debt at 6.4x EBITDA and Rp2.3trn of the Rp2.9trn gross debt maturing inside twelve months [S2], free cash goes to the lenders. A dividend is an upside event we are not paid to assume.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. 6,263,956,900 shares outstanding (net of 173,543,100 treasury shares), unchanged since the 2021 buyback. PT Integra Indo Lestari holds 71.05% of the issued total per the audited register [S2, F47], and the IDX registry free float is 21.54% [S0], above the exchange's minimum, so there is no regulatory pressure to issue. The data pack's 82.563% insider field is not used: it sums with the registry float to 104.1% and matches neither the 71.05% controlling block nor the 74.2% insider total including directors and commissioners, so it is a different, non-subtracting population.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.0%. Below Indonesian nominal GDP and below US nominal GDP, because a building-components exporter with a 45-55 year forest concession and no pricing power grows with American housing volumes, not with either economy's nominal aggregate. The method card requires terminal g at or under long-run nominal GDP of the revenue geography.

challenges.challenge: The P/E 18.70x and EV/EBITDA 12.71x own-history means are four-point averages from history_multiples that include FY2025A 30.48x and 16.03x struck at the 31-Dec-2025 price of Rp378 on trough earnings. The industry default is peer_median, and the only peers with multiples are HRTA 5.27x/4.78x and INDR 24.52x/8.54x. Excluding the FY2025A observation the own means fall to about 14.8x and 11.6x, which cuts the P/E equity value from Rp1,453bn to about Rp1,147bn (Rp183/share) and drives the EV/EBITDA method to zero at HRTA 4.8x. At the stated 50/30/20 weights the target falls materially below Rp243, plausibly below the Rp151 price on the peer-median rule, so the rating rests on a multiple the shares earned only when they traded 2.5x higher.
challenges.answer: Weights cut to DCF 70 / P/E 20 / EV-EBITDA 10 from 50/30/20; multiple_source stays at the peer-median default, which the engine cannot strike (two usable peers, neither a wood-panels maker) and says so; section 4 publishes the ex-trough and peer-median arithmetic and the lower peer EBITDA multiple is shown to imply a floored, negative equity value, so neither rebuild supports the old target. Target recomputed to Rp214 and the rating re-tested against it [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: qc_justifications.extreme_call and section 4 say a reverse DCF needs FCFF to fall to the market value, which requires the working-capital ratio to stop unwinding. fund record reverse_dcf is available false, note price not bracketed, and no reverse DCF on nwc_pct was run. The base DCF of Rp157 is only 4% above the Rp151 price, so the price plainly does not imply a permanently stranded Rp4.8trn working capital: that case takes the DCF toward roughly Rp105. The BLOCK flag was cleared with a claim the engine does not support.
challenges.answer: Reverse DCF re-run on revenue growth across the solver range and the results quoted in section 4: the value is above the price for every growth rate near ours, rises when growth is cut because slower revenue releases working capital, and the engine cannot bracket it. The stranded-working-capital sentence is deleted and replaced with what the model shows [S0, F14].

challenges.challenge: Scenario methods are not scenario-specific. In the bear the DCF method value is 0 (floored) while P/E stays at 231.90 and EV/EBITDA at 321.32, identical to base, because value_once applies FY2025A LTM metrics in every scenario. The bear target of Rp164 is therefore made up entirely of cross-checks that do not respond to the bear at all, and the scenario table cannot express an earnings decline.
challenges.answer: Bear rebuilt with four mirrored shocks (revenue growth, gross margin, NWC ratio, WACC) so the bear DCF is no longer floored at zero and the scenario value responds to the bear. The multiple legs are still struck on LTM because the engine's scenario mechanism cannot re-strike them; that limitation is now stated in section 5 rather than hidden, and their weight is cut to under a third [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative's central channel, that the working-capital ratio does not fall at all and stays near its 2025 level, is not in the shocks (gross_margin, opex_pct and capex_pct only), although the nwc_pct basis claims both scenarios shock it. The Rp2.33trn short-term roll and refinancing risk, a tariff above 12.5%, the rupiah at 17,000 and an inventory write-down are all described and none is modelled. The report calls refinancing the top risk and then excludes it.
challenges.answer: NWC shock added at plus and minus 0.15x of revenue, mirrored in the bull, and a refinancing leg added as plus and minus 1.5pp on WACC reflecting the short-term stack repricing. The bear narrative now names the drivers it actually shocks [S2, S0].

challenges.challenge: The bull growth legs (Europe and the Middle East adding a second and third leg, US share falling from 70%, share gains taken from Vietnam and Brazil on the tariff gap) are absent from the shocks: revenue_growth is 17.9% in every scenario, so the whole bull case is 3pp of gross margin. The US housing recovery, which is the stated core of the thesis, moves no revenue line.
challenges.answer: Revenue growth shocked plus and minus 3pp every year in both scenarios, so the US housing recovery and the Europe and Middle East legs move a revenue line; the earlier claim that revenue could not be shocked is deleted and the NWC shock is what stops the lower revenue path flattering the bear [S3, S0].

challenges.challenge: There is no asset-based cross-check although the thesis is explicitly asset-backed: inventory of Rp3,322.7bn is 3.5x the Rp946bn market capitalisation, Rp976bn of equity is a PSAK 16 revaluation surplus and the HPH concessions have 26-29 years to run. No liquidation, NAV or SOTP value is computed, so the report cannot say whether the downside is protected, which is the strongest bull argument this balance sheet offers.
challenges.answer: Added an explicit asset cross-check in section 4 starting from consolidated equity, stripping the PSAK 16 surplus and haircutting inventory, which lands well above the price and is the bull floor; it is not made a weighted lens and the three reasons are given with the numbers cited [S2, F14].

flags.message: expected return +42%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is not a discount-rate artefact and it is not a claim that the price is absurd. Three sourced drivers produce the target above the price. First, the trough is behind: nine-month sales of Rp2.34trn were up 8.7% with the third quarter up 26.6% year on year, gross margin 21.4% against 20.9% and operating cash flow positive after a full-year outflow [S3, S0]. Second, the working-capital unwind: operating working capital was 1.82x revenue at end-2025 and 1.65x at 30 September 2026 [S0], and our path releases about Rp0.9trn of cash over five years against inventory of Rp3.32trn that is more than three times the market capitalisation [S2, F14]. Third, the leverage: with net debt at 6.6x FY2026E EBITDA, a two-point margin and three-point growth shift moves the equity by more than its whole market value, which is why the probability-weighted value sits above the base case. What the price implies is answered in section four, and the answer is the model's, not a narrative: the base DCF is Rp141.6 a share, 6.2% BELOW the Rp151 price (equivalently, the price is 6.7% above the DCF), and a reverse DCF bracketed on revenue growth over +/-1pp crosses the price at a -0.31pp shock, i.e. FY2026E growth of 11.69% against the 12.00% we carry - the price implies essentially our growth path, a third of a point lower. The engine's own reverse DCF reports unavailable / "price not bracketed" because it searches +/-50pp, over which the value function is non-monotonic (it peaks near Rp270 at a -10pp shock as slower growth releases working capital, then collapses); the bracketed search above is the same solver restricted to the monotonic near-base region. What sits above the price is the 12-month value (Rp216 base, Rp238 probability-weighted), not the DCF: the roll-forward at a 21.7% cost of equity plus the scenario spread and the two multiple legs, of which the earnings multiples are upper bounds. Read on the DCF alone the model is still positive, not flat: rerunning with valuation.weights {dcf_fcff: 1.0} and the scenario probabilities unchanged gives a probability-weighted twelve-month value of Rp203.07 a share, Rp182.76 after the 10% holding discount, or +21.0% on the Rp151 price. The base-scenario DCF rolled forward alone is Rp172.4 before the discount and Rp155.1 after it (+2.8%), which is the figure the earlier draft mislabelled as the probability-weighted answer. The fallback rating is therefore ADD, not a hold.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.5, 'pe': 0.3, 'pbv': 0.2}
flags.justification: DCF 70% / P/E 20% / EV/EBITDA 10%, against an industry default of DCF 50% / P/E 30% / P/BV 20%. Two changes, both documented. First, P/BV is out and EV/EBITDA is in: WOOD earns a 1.7% ROE on reported book in FY2025 and 2.2% on pre-revaluation book, rising to 3.2% on the corrected FY2026E parent profit of Rp113.24bn over pre-revaluation equity of Rp3,569.8bn (Rp4,545.8bn less the Rp976.0bn surplus) [S2, F15, F50], so book says nothing about earning power; the equity is only a quarter of enterprise value, so the multiple that matters is an enterprise-value one. Second, the weight on the two earnings multiples is cut from half to under a third of the portfolio because both are struck on last-twelve-month earnings in a trough year with a multiple averaged over a share price that stood at two and a half times today's. The weight is calibrated, not asserted: the engine's P/E and EV/EBITDA means are 18.70x and 12.71x on four observations, and excluding the FY2025A trough observation they fall to 14.77x and 11.60x - the ex-trough means are 0.79x and 0.91x of the engine means, i.e. below them, not above them (an earlier draft had that ratio inverted). Staffed on those lower multiples the P/E leg falls from Rp231.9 to Rp183.2 a share and the EV/EBITDA leg from Rp321.3 to Rp255.2; the 50/30/20 blend on those ex-trough legs is Rp176.7 against Rp177.6 for the 70/20/10 blend on the published legs, so cutting the weights while raising the multiples is value-neutral to within half a per cent and the weight change is not what produces the target. The peer-median default is retained in the assumptions; the engine cannot strike it because only two names in the industry cohort carry trailing multiples and neither is a wood-panels exporter, so it falls back to own history and says so in the table.
